content:
Earlier this year, I swapped my battery-powered mower for a robot mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. You can manually drive it around the perimeter of your yard to create a virtual map. Once set up, it automatically starts mowing according to a preset schedule.

I had also previously tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think it may be a simpler choice for many people.

Automatic camera mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 that I reviewed earlier this year lies in how the two machines understand your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses RTK base station positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower around the perimeter with my iPhone to build the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. Equipped with three cameras, the mower can automatically map out the lawn and navigate, without the need to bury boundary wires or install an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process does indeed take longer. However, for people who aren't particularly fond of tinkering with technology, this method may be easier to get started with.

To test this idea, I asked my mom, who lives in another state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without any help from me. She replied that everything worked smoothly. That said, it's harder for me to know whether she'd have the patience to first manually drive the mower around the entire perimeter, and then manually mark the areas to avoid.

The automatic mapping did cause one small issue in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbor's lawn, so TerraMow initially incorporated part of my neighbor's lawn into my map.

I later resolved this by setting that area as a no-go zone in the app. That said, if your lawn doesn't have a clear visual boundary, you'll need to pay special attention during the initial mapping.

Remote camera viewing via the app

TerraMow's cameras also make one of my favourite features possible. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to keep this view open in a large window. I could work indoors while watching the mower move around the backyard from its perspective.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun and can occasionally explain why it slows down or avoids certain things. The Anthbot M9 doesn't have a similar camera view feature.

The two iPhone apps have a lot in common. Both can schedule working times, adjust mowing behaviour, divide zones, mark no-go zones, and remotely control the mower.

Speaking of that last feature, TerraMow has a particularly outstanding design detail. In addition to the traditional left-right virtual controls, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually controlling the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule, without any intervention. However, using TerraMow's joystick to touch up spots that were missed is genuinely a pleasure.

Sometimes I almost feel like I'm controlling the robot with telekinesis (and it feels really great). I can hold my iPhone at my side, gently move my thumb to "walk," and the mower follows my directions.

Every robot mower app should take cues from this control design.

More aggressive mowing performance

The TerraMow V1000's mowing performance is also more aggressive than the Anthbot M9's. During testing, it cut lower and was noticeably louder while working.

I wouldn't say the TerraMow is loud. But the difference between the two is obvious. The Anthbot can run so quietly that you almost forget it's still there, even when it's mowing at night with its headlights on.

Because TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. Therefore, scheduling daytime runs becomes more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and well-made. It's also bigger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that can cover the charging dock, whereas Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has performed consistently and reliably. I've relied on it for several consecutive weeks and haven't had to cut the grass myself since.

When adaptive mapping is too "smart"

The visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts the map based on what it sees. After each job is completed, saving these changes takes a little time, during which you temporarily can't do anything else in the app.

After a few days of rain, I ran into an interesting quirk. Puddles formed in parts of the yard, and TerraMow cleverly avoided those areas on its next run.

The grass within the skipped circular patches later grew taller. After some time had passed, the mower seemed to treat this patch of tall grass as something to keep avoiding, so even after the ground dried, that patch of grass continued to be ignored.

I used the remote control function in the app to manually mow that patch of tall grass, and the problem was resolved. Once the grass returned to normal, automatic mowing resumed working properly there.

Regular edging can also help TerraMow operate closer to the boundaries. If you don't trim, tall grass near the edges may be mistaken for obstacles rather than mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive and more reliant on the boundaries and obstacles I set up myself. This method requires more upfront work, but it can avoid situations where the map "changes its mind" and refuses to mow a certain patch of grass.

9to5Mac Opinion

After using both systems, for most people, I lean toward TerraMow's camera approach.

For me, burying boundary wires is completely out of the question, and installing an RTK base station means one more piece of hardware to place, power, and maintain. TerraMow needs neither.

Its visual navigation isn't perfect. Initial mapping takes longer, indistinct boundaries require manual correction, and adaptive behaviour has mistakenly treated overly tall grass as a permanent obstacle.

These issues remain manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, fun real-time camera footage, and the best manual controls I've seen in any robot mower app.

I really enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing that part over to a robot means I can spend more time on landscaping, edging, and detail work, while keeping the lawn neat.

The TerraMow V1000 delivers on this, so I can recommend it, especially for people who want a robot mower but don't want to bury boundary wires, install an RTK antenna, or manually walk the entire yard with an iPhone.

Amazon is currently selling the TerraMow V1000 with a promo code. After entering the $200 promo code on the website, the price drops to $999. You can also purchase it on TerraMow's official website.
